summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for $facet; source-anchored research pack.

facts.text: 7. Independent coverage dated 2017-01-19 records the pre-`$facet` state of the art that motivated the stage: before 3.4 a developer had to "either re-structure your data specifically for faceted search or execute a separate aggregation for every single individual 'facet' you want to filter by." <https://thecodebarbarian.com/a-nodejs-perspective-on-mongodb-34-facet.html>

11. The server source describes the stage as blocking and single-output: "A $facet stage contains multiple sub-pipelines. Each input to the $facet stage will feed into each of the sub-pipelines. The $facet stage is blocking, and outputs only one document, containing an array of results for each sub-pipeline." <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.h>

4. `$facet` emits exactly one document and then EOF, regardless of input cardinality. The stage's own class comment: "A $facet stage contains multiple sub-pipelines. Each input to the $facet stage will feed into each of the sub-pipelines. The $facet stage is blocking, and outputs only one document, containing an array of results for each sub-pipeline." (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.h)

6. `$facet` is built from three cooperating parts: a single `TeeBuffer` that holds input, one `DocumentSourceTeeConsumer` prepended as the initial source of each sub-pipeline, and the `DocumentSourceFacet` stage that drains them. The constructor wires each sub-pipeline with `facet.pipeline->addInitialSource(DocumentSourceTeeConsumer::create(expCtx, facetId, kTeeConsumerStageName));`, indexing the consumer by `facetId`. (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp)

17. `LookupRequirement::kAllowed` and `UnionRequirement::kAllowed` mean the exclusion is one-directional: `$facet` may not contain another `$facet`, but `$facet` may itself appear inside a `$lookup` or `$unionWith` sub-pipeline. (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp)

The strongest convergence: four independent searches all found disconfirming evidence against the stage's own stated rationale. "Input documents are passed only once" is a true mechanism description and *not* a performance guarantee — two community threads measure it slower for paginate-with-count, and Payload CMS deleted its `$facet` code path outright.

Explicitly **out of scope** (separate frontier items): the Atlas Search `facet` *collector* and the `$searchMeta` stage, which are a different mechanism that happens to share the word "facet"; the sibling bucketing stages `$bucket`, `$bucketAuto`, `$sortByCount`; and the generic aggregation-pipeline memory model except where `$facet` deviates from it.

**C7. The hoist-the-`$match` workaround is not always expressible.** SERVER-30474 (open, Backlog, filed 2017-08-02, 9 votes) records that combining several sub-pipeline predicates into one leading `$match` with `$or` does not preserve selectivity. Commenter Kevin Pulo: "When run as independent aggregations, these each scan just 1 document. But when run as above inside `$facet`, the whole collection gets scanned." The requested fix — planning each sub-pipeline fully, "like the way that `$lookup` with a pipeline does" — remains unimplemented as of this report.

13. The "parallel" execution described in popular write-ups is interleaved, not concurrent. Input is distributed through an internal `TeeBuffer` stage (`$internalFacetTeeConsumer`) that "will batch incoming documents and allow each consumer to consume one batch at a time," and "consumers must be able to pause their execution to allow other consumers to process the batch before moving to the next batch." <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/tee_buffer.h> The widely repeated framing of `$facet` as "`async.parallel()` for aggregation pipelines" therefore d

26. The manual states the rule plainly: "If the `$facet` stage is the first stage in a pipeline, the stage will perform a `COLLSCAN`. The `$facet` stage does not make use of indexes if it is the first stage in the pipeline." If it comes later and earlier stages used indexes, it will not trigger a `COLLSCAN`. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/>

Two naming collisions are worth stating once, because they poison searches on this topic. First, `facet` in MongoDB Search (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/facet/) is a different operator with different semantics from the aggregation-pipeline `$facet` documented at https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/. Second, "sub-pipeline" here means an entry in the `$facet` specification object, not a `$lookup` or `$unionWith` pipeline.

25. This is an optimizer gap, not a semantic necessity, and it is a known open ticket. SERVER-30474, "leading $facet with each facet beginning with $match should add $match before $facet", proposes hoisting the sub-pipelines' common `$match` predicates above `$facet` so the planner can use an index; it remains unresolved in the backlog with no fix version, and states that "$facet is not smart enough to use an index" because "the planning system will simply default to a COLLSCAN". (https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-30474)

26. Users hit this in practice and it was triaged as the same gap. SERVER-34428, "$facet aggregation stage does not use index created for the sub pipelines in it and perform COLLSCAN instead", reports sub-pipelines scanning where the identical queries used indexes when run separately; it was closed as a duplicate of SERVER-30474 with no fix version. (https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-34428)

This report covers how teams actually run `$facet` in production: what it is used for, the limits it imposes, how to measure whether it is helping, and what to use instead when it is not. It stays on the `$facet` stage itself. Sibling stages (`$bucket`, `$bucketAuto`, `$sortByCount`, `$unionWith`, `$setWindowFields`, `$searchMeta`) appear only where they are the direct alternative to `$facet` or are named by the `$facet` documentation. The general aggregation framework, the Atlas Search index format, and sharded-cluster pipeline splitting are out of scope.

26. `$facet` buys atomicity of input (one consistent snapshot feeds every facet) and one round trip. It does not buy parallelism (claim 8) and does not reliably buy speed (claims 17, 20). Choose it when a single consistent input set across all facets matters, or when round trips are expensive; do not choose it as a default performance optimisation. 27. `$facet` is a poor fit for large result payloads (16 MiB ceiling, no disk spill) and for pipelines that must write (`$out` and `$merge` are banned). It is a good fit for bounded summary output: counts, buckets, top-N lists. ([docs](https://www.m

5. In that single output document, each sub-pipeline's results appear as an array under its output field name — an array of documents, even when the sub-pipeline yields zero or one document. (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/, https://studio3t.com/knowledge-base/articles/mongodb-facet-bucket-stages/)

Neither of the other two had read `document_source_facet.h`. - **One report's methodology is undercut by another's finding.** `edge-cases.md` infers the restriction list is "stable across 7.0 → current" because the current and v7.0 manual pages match. `history.md` establishes that

21. That counter is initialised once before the facet loop and is never reset per facet, so the 100 MB ceiling applies to the **sum** of all sub-pipeline outputs, not to any one sub-pipeline. (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/r7.0.0/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp)

**Saturation: reached on contract, restrictions and the index problem; not reached on performance.** The reports recycle the same primary sources, which is the diminishing-returns signal. The one open question worth more work is D4 (faster or slower?), and it can't be closed by more searching — the same reporter measured `$facet` 3× *slower* in the .NET driver and ~10× *faster* in the Robo3T shell, which points at driver-side deserialisation as an uncontrolled variable. That needs a controlled benchmark run, not another report.

- **Done** — Read all four `$facet` reports; produced a synthesis with 58 tagged claims, 8 side-by-side disagreements, 7 cross-report corrections, a per-area saturation table, and a 40-URL source list. - **Decided** — Resolved the "parallel?" dispute as a terminology conflict (one input pass ≠ concurrency); resolved the sharded-merge gap from the source tree; left the 100 MB scope, the error code, and the performance direction open with both sides stated. - **State** — Repo `llms-explorer` untouched, branch `chore/sync-optimizer-skills` still clean; output written only to the hub research run

**Concept:** `$facet` (MongoDB aggregation pipeline stage) **Parent:** `mongodb-aggregation-stages-deep` **Report date:** 2026-09-18 **Research objective:** boundary conditions, failure modes, disagreements, disconfirming evidence.

**C1. The `$facet` output document is a single BSON document and is therefore capped at 16 MiB; exceeding it fails the aggregation.** Because every sub-pipeline's entire result is materialised as an array field inside one output document, total result volume — not per-document size — is what hits the ceiling. "The final output document is subject to the 16 mebibyte BSON document size limit. If it exceeds 16 mebibytes, the aggregation produces an error."

**C2. Each stage inside a `$facet` is additionally capped at 100 MB of intermediate result, raising `ExceededMemoryLimit` (error code 146).** "As each stage in a `$facet` executes, the resulting document is limited to 100 megabytes... If a `$facet` stage constructs a document where the size exceeds the 100 megabyte limit, MongoDB returns an `ExceededMemoryLimit` error."

**C3. `allowDiskUse` does not relax the `$facet` limit, because `$facet` cannot spill to disk.** This is a genuine asymmetry: `$group`, `$sort`, `$bucket`, `$bucketAuto`, `$setWindowFields` and `$sortByCount` all spill when `allowDiskUse` is true; `$facet` does not, so a sub-pipeline containing an otherwise-spillable `$group` still dies at 100 MB. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/ and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits/

**C9. `$facet` cannot be nested, and a fixed set of stages is banned inside its sub-pipelines.** Disallowed: `$collStats`, `$facet`, `$geoNear`, `$indexStats`, `$out`, `$merge`, `$planCacheStats`, `$search`, `$searchMeta`, `$vectorSearch`. The same list appears in both the current manual and the v7.0 manual, so this set is stable across at least 7.0 → current. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/ and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v7.0/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/

**C11. Sub-pipelines are mutually invisible: one sub-pipeline's output cannot feed another within the same `$facet`.** "These sub-pipelines are completely independent of one another... The output of one sub-pipeline can not be used as the input for a different sub-pipeline within the same `$facet` stage." Cross-facet arithmetic must be done in stages placed *after* the `$facet`.

**C13. `$facet` is a blocking stage: it consumes its entire input before emitting anything.** It is grouped with `$group`, `$bucket`, `$bucketAuto`, `$count` and `$sortByCount` as a blocking stage, with the author noting "it's a stretch to call `$facet` a group stage, but in the context of this topic, it's best to think of it that way". Consequence: no streaming, no early `$limit` short-circuit, and latency is bounded by the slowest sub-pipeline.

10. Sub-pipelines are independent and cannot feed one another; each receives the identical input set, and further processing must happen in stages placed after `$facet`. <https://docs.huihoo.com/mongodb/3.4/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/index.html>

18. The `$merge`-inside-`$facet` prohibition is observable in the wild as the server error "$merge is not allowed to be used within a $facet stage." <https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/issues/11630>

22. The current manual states the resulting rule: "As each stage in a `$facet` executes, the resulting document is limited to 100 megabytes," and exceeding it returns `ExceededMemoryLimit` (error code 146). <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/>

23. `allowDiskUse` does not relax that cap: "the `allowDiskUse` flag doesn't affect the 100 megabyte size limit, since `$facet` can't spill to disk." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/>

25. The two limits interact: a `$facet` document may legally reach 100 MB in-flight yet still fail downstream, because "any final documents in an aggregation pipeline's result set face a hard 16MB BSON size limit." <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-40317>

29. The premise of `$facet` — one pass over the input beats N queries — does not hold for the most common real-world use, count-plus-page pagination. A 2024 community thread measured two separate queries at about 47 ms against a single `$facet` query at about 72 ms on the same data. <https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/why-is-facet-so-slow/298075>

30. The explanation offered in that thread is eager fetching: "without the $facet, only 10 documents are FETCHed. With the $facet all matching documents [20,464] are FETCHed even if none are required for the count." The reporter moved to `$unionWith` for better performance. This is a community explanation, not a MongoDB staff statement or documented behavior. <https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/why-is-facet-so-slow/298075>

- <https://www.percona.com/blog/2016/12/13/mongodb-3-4-facet-aggregation-features-and-server-27395-mongod-crash/> — Percona, 2016-12-13 - <https://thecodebarbarian.com/a-nodejs-perspective-on-mongodb-34-facet.html> — Valeri Karpov, 2017-01-19 - <https://mongoing.com/docs/reference/operator/aggregation/facet.html> — 3.4 manual mirror - <https://docs.huihoo.com/mongodb/3.4/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/index.html> — 3.4 manual mirror - <https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/issues/11630> — observed `$merge`-in-`$facet` error text

16. `FacetRequirement::kNotAllowed` is what makes `$facet` non-nestable, and it is enforced at parse time with error `40600` and the message "is not allowed to be used within a $facet stage". (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp)

19. In a sharded cluster the stage is not splittable across shards. The `distributedPlanLogic` comment states: "The $facet stage must be run on the merging shard." (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.h) Additionally, the stage escalates to router execution when any sub-pipeline demands it, and rejects the contradictory case with an `IllegalOperation` error: "$facet pipeline '...' must run on router, but '...' requires a shard". (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/master/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp)

20. The accumulated output is capped at `_maxOutputDocSizeBytes` (100 MB by default, claim 14), checked incrementally as documents arrive via a closure over a running `usedBytes` counter, with `uassert(4031700, ... "document constructed by $facet is " << usedBytes << " bytes, which exceeds the limit of " << maxBytes << " bytes")`. (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/r7.0.0/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp)

22. `allowDiskUse` does not raise this ceiling: "Note the allowDiskUse flag doesn't affect the 100 megabyte size limit, since `$facet` can't spill to disk." (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/) This follows from `DiskUseRequirement::kNoDiskUse` in claim 15. Note the contrast with ordinary blocking stages, where `allowDiskUse: true` does lift the 100 MB RAM limit at a large latency cost. (https://www.practical-mongodb-aggregations.com/guides/performance.html)

23. A second, harder ceiling sits above the first: "The final output document is subject to the 16 mebibyte BSON document size limit. If it exceeds 16 mebibytes, the aggregation produces an error." (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/) Because 16 MiB < 100 MB, the BSON limit is the binding constraint for any `$facet` whose result is returned to a client as a document; the 100 MB knob only binds when the pipeline continues and reshapes the result before it is returned.

24. A leading `$facet` cannot use indexes: "If the `$facet` stage is the first stage in a pipeline, the stage will perform a `COLLSCAN`. The `$facet` stage does not make use of indexes if it is the first stage in the pipeline." (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/)

27. The limit is positional, and moving `$facet` later in the pipeline recovers index use for the *preceding* stages: "If the `$facet` stage comes later in the pipeline and earlier stages have used indexes, `$facet` will not trigger a `COLLSCAN` during execution." (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/) Combined with claims 24–26, this is the single most consequential practical rule for the stage: filter before `$facet`, never only inside it.

28. The "one pass is cheaper" intuition (claim 3) is therefore not a performance guarantee, and at least one production framework removed the stage over it. Payload CMS deprecated its `useFacet` option with the comment "@deprecated Payload doesn't use `$facet` anymore anywhere", replacing `$facet`-based paginate-with-count by direct `countDocuments()` / `estimatedDocumentCount()` calls plus reordered sort/skip/limit ahead of `$lookup`. (https://github.com/payloadcms/payload/commit/d4d2bf4)

2. **Whether the 100 MB limit is per stage or per stage-total.** The manual scopes it per executing stage — "As each stage in a `$facet` executes, the resulting document is limited to 100 megabytes" (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/) — whereas the `usedBytes` accumulator is shared across the whole facet loop, making it a total (claim 21). Code is the stronger evidence here, but the two readings differ materially for a `$facet` with many medium-sized outputs.

Met. Six independent hosts were used — `mongodb.com` (official manual), `raw.githubusercontent.com` / `github.com` (primary source code, `master` and `r7.0.0`), `jira.mongodb.org` (issue tracker), `practical-mongodb-aggregations.com` (independent reference book), `studio3t.com` (independent vendor documentation), and a third-party production codebase (`github.com/payloadcms`). Disconfirming evidence was sought and found: the official "input passed only once" efficiency framing is undercut by the COLLSCAN limitation in SERVER-30474 / SERVER-34428, by a community benchmark measuring `$facet` slo

1. `$facet` runs several sub-pipelines over one input document stream and returns a single document whose fields each hold that sub-pipeline's results as an array. ([docs](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/)) 2. Every sub-pipeline receives the identical input set. A sub-pipeline cannot read another sub-pipeline's output inside the same stage. ([docs](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/)) 3. MongoDB documents `$bucket`, `$bucketAuto`, and `$sortByCount` as the stages designed for use inside `$facet` sub-pipelines. ([do

13. Current documentation: if `$facet` is the first stage of the pipeline it performs a `COLLSCAN` and uses no index; if earlier stages used indexes, `$facet` does not trigger a `COLLSCAN`. ([docs](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/)) 14. The MongoDB 4.4 manual said the opposite and stronger thing: "The `$facet` stage, and its sub-pipelines, cannot make use of indexes, even if its sub-pipelines use `$match` or if `$facet` is the first stage in the pipeline. The `$facet` stage will always perform a `COLLSCAN` during execution." ([4.4 manual mirror](https:/

24. Separately and independently, the final output document is bound by the 16 mebibyte BSON document size limit; exceeding it errors the aggregation. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/>

**C4. The 100 MB cap is version-gated: before the fix in SERVER-40317, `$facet` had no memory bound at all.** SERVER-40317, "$facet execution has no limit on how much memory it can consume", was filed 2019-03-22 and fixed in 3.6.20, 4.0.21, 4.2.10, 4.4.2 and 4.7.0. On any server older than those patch releases, an oversized `$facet` exhausts server memory rather than returning `ExceededMemoryLimit`. Diagnosing a `$facet` OOM therefore requires knowing the exact patch version, not just the major version.

**C12. A sub-pipeline ending in `$count` returns an empty array — not zero — when nothing matches.** Reported shape was `{ scoreRank: [] }` where `{ scoreRank: [{ count: 2 }] }` was expected, for the pipeline `{ $facet: { scoreRank: [ { $match: { 'quizzes.0.score': { $gt: 0 } } }, { $count: 'count' } ] } }`. Downstream `$arrayElemAt` on that empty array returns *missing*, not `0`, so totals silently vanish from the response instead of reading zero. Guard with `$ifNull`. Sources: https://github.com/Automattic/mongoose/issues/9317 and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggreg

**D1. "Does `$facet` use indexes?" — the official docs invite a misreading.** The manual says "If the `$facet` stage comes later in the pipeline and earlier stages have used indexes, `$facet` will not trigger a `COLLSCAN` during execution." Read loosely, that suggests `$facet` itself becomes index-aware once it is not first. SERVER-30474 shows it does not: sub-pipeline predicates are never planned against indexes regardless of position. The two statements are reconcilable — the index work is done entirely by the pre-`$facet` stages, and `$facet` merely inherits whatever document stream they pr

**D2. Is the one-pass efficiency claim borne out in practice? Disconfirming evidence exists but is not decisive.** The manual's rationale is that "Input documents are passed to the `$facet` stage only once", implying a `$facet` beats N separate round-trips. A community benchmark of paging-with-count measured the opposite: `$facet` averaged **1724 ms** (range 1685–1823 ms) against **553.2 ms** (range 535–579 ms) for a separate `count` plus `skip`/`limit` — roughly 3× slower over 10 iterations. The benchmark is not authoritative: a responder flagged a missing `$sort` ("If you do not sort you mig

**D3. Sharded-cluster merge behaviour for `$facet` is undocumented.** Secondary write-ups assert that `$facet`, as a blocking stage, forces a merge off the shards. The official sharded-aggregation page does **not** name `$facet`: its stated exceptions to merging on `mongos` are only `$out`, `$lookup` against an unsharded collection, and sorting/grouping stages with `allowDiskUse` enabled. **Gap:** I could not confirm from a primary source where a `$facet` merge runs, nor whether `$facet` counts as a "grouping stage" for the random-merge-shard rule. SERVER-40317, "$facet execution has no limit on how much memory it can consume," was created 2019-03-22 and asked that "the $facet should return an error as soon as it has >100MB of results, rather than waiting until it's computed all of its data." <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-40317>

18. Ten stages are rejected inside `$facet` sub-pipelines: `$collStats`, `$facet`, `$geoNear`, `$indexStats`, `$out`, `$merge`, `$planCacheStats`, `$search`, `$searchMeta`, `$vectorSearch`. (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/) The set is coherent rather than arbitrary: each excluded stage either must be first in a pipeline (`$collStats`, `$indexStats`, `$geoNear`, `$search`, `$vectorSearch`, `$planCacheStats`) or must be last and is a sink (`$out`, `$merge`) — neither position is available to a sub-pipeline whose first slot is occupied by the injected tee

1. **Which error a 100 MB overflow surfaces as.** The manual says "If a `$facet` stage constructs a document where the size exceeds the 100 megabyte limit, MongoDB returns an `ExceededMemoryLimit` error" (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/), but the accumulation check in `doGetNext()` raises bare `uassert` code `4031700`, not `ExceededMemoryLimit` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mongodb/mongo/r7.0.0/src/mongo/db/pipeline/document_source_facet.cpp). The likeliest reconciliation is that the documented `ExceededMemoryLimit` comes from blocking stages *ins

3. **Magnitude and cause of the pagination slowdown.** A community benchmark reports `$facet` at ~1724 ms average against ~553 ms for separate simple queries, roughly 3x slower — yet the same reporter saw `$facet` win by ~10x from the Robo3T shell, pointing at the .NET driver (2.12.3) rather than the server, and a responder challenged the methodology (missing `$sort`, a possibly redundant query in the comparison arm, and a fixed skip offset that is not real pagination) (https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/paging-with-count-performance-facet-vs-simple-query/170806). Direction of the effe

1. `$facet` takes an object whose keys are output field names and whose values are arrays of aggregation stages: `{ $facet: { <outputField1>: [ <stage1>, ... ], ... } }`. (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/facet/)

2. Every sub-pipeline receives the identical set of documents that reached the `$facet` stage. The docs state: "Each sub-pipeline within `$facet` is passed the exact same set of input documents.
